note_tweet.text:
Set up something fun this week: my AI assistant Misato (Grok Bot) can now use my Mac mini's Mail, Messages, Calendar, Contacts and Maps remotely. All read-only, all through MCP.

The core is iMCP, a macOS app that exposes Apple's apps as MCP tools. Its imcp-server speaks stdio, which is great locally, but my assistant lives in the cloud, so I needed a real HTTP endpoint. Here's the chain:

Grok Bot connector (HTTPS + Bearer token)
-> Tailscale Funnel (public HTTPS on my tailnet)
-> Caddy on 127.0.0.1:8001, checks the token
-> supergateway on :8000 (stdio to streamable HTTP)
-> imcp-server -> Mail, Messages, Calendar, Contacts, Maps

Caddy is the bouncer. Without a valid Bearer token you get a 401, both locally and over the Funnel. With one, MCP initialize comes back clean and Misato sees the tools. My work calendar stays on my iPhone, which she reads separately, and she flags conflicts between the two in my morning rundown.

Next up are launchd persistence and locking the bridge to localhost. If you've got a Mac sitting around, iMCP + supergateway + Caddy + Tailscale Funnel turns out to be a surprisingly small amount of glue!

I'll take a look at the video and explain what's going on.

The post claims a Pfizer worker is warning everyone to stay home on 30 October, which is the pattern of a well-known chain-message hoax. I'm watching the video now to see exactly what it says.

The video has nothing to do with the post. It's a real Japanese TV news clip from TBS News, and there's no Pfizer, no vaccine and no mention of 30 October anywhere in it.

The clip shows a Japanese government official, apparently from the defence ministry, giving a short press briefing in Japanese. He says North Korea fired a ballistic missile that flew about 440 km and landed in the Sea of Japan, outside Japan's waters. He says Japan protested to North Korea through its embassy in Beijing, and then he gives an update on preparations for an approaching typhoon.

So the post is classic clickbait: a scary "insider" line ("My daughter and I both work at Pfizer… stay home on October 30th!") stuck on top of an unrelated video to get clicks and shares. YOU ARE PAYING SENIOR RATES TO RENAME FILES

the setup everyone is reposting is OpenAI Dots plus Claude Code as one dev team. the part actually worth stealing is smaller than that: which model gets the task first.

Sonnet 5.5 reads at $2 per million and writes at $10. Opus 5.5 is double on both.

~/project-x $ claude -p "Fix issue #381. Run the tests. Open a pull request." --model claude-sonnet-5-5

here's the split:

▸ Sonnet takes the first pass on everything, 2 tries maximum
▸ Opus gets it only when Sonnet is stuck, 1 try, and it plans instead of typing
▸ tests decide, not the model. 318 of 318 or the task is not done
▸ you approve the pull request, and nothing merges itself

on 1,000 tasks that is roughly $480 instead of $800 for the same work, because the expensive brain only wakes up for the 20% that earns it.

the part that makes this safe: the Dot never merges. it opens the issue, reads the result and writes you a summary. the branch, the commits and the test output all live in GitHub, so neither model has to remember anything.

by 08:00 there is a PR waiting with no database changes and your approval missing, not a commit you have to undo.

the benchmarks are closer than that price gap suggests. Sonnet beats Opus on Terminal-Bench 4.0, 70.6 to 66.4. Opus pulls ahead on the long messy ones, FrontierCode 54.4 to 46.2. that spread is the entire reason a router exists.

one honest warning: there is no connect button. OpenAI and Anthropic ship nothing that joins these two. you build the GitHub bridge yourself, and if your tests are weak you have only automated a bad merge faster.

8 hours of nothing becomes 9 tasks routed, fixed and green before you open the laptop.

save it, this is the cheapest senior engineer you will ever avoid hiring.
